title: FarmTable: where the philosophy becomes food
vimeoName: Module 7 - FarmTable: where the philosophy becomes food

segments.text: If crevaryl has a soul, you can taste it, literally.
This module is about the farm table and about food,
which, if you know me at all,
you know is the part of this project
I could talk about for six hours instead of 10 minutes.
I'll restrain myself.
Let me start with the philosophy,
and it fits in one sentence.
Before the plate, there is a grower.
Everything else follows from that.
Over 70% of what we serve is grown on this property.
The vegetables ripened in our soil.
The herbs were cut this morning.
The eggs were laid today.
By hens, you can walk over and meet.
What we don't grow, we source as close as possible.
Cheeses from the region, fish from this coast,
wines from Alentejo,
and from the Vicentino vineyards up the road,
medroneo from the local distillery.
The menu rotates with the seasons
because the farm rotates with the seasons.
And that's not a limitation, it's the entire point.
A tomato in August here
tastes like a different food
from a supermarket tomato in January.
Our guests come, in part,
to remember what food actually tastes like.
This is what root to table means when we say it.
Not a marketing garnish.
A supply chain you can walk in five minutes.
Breakfast.
I said it before and I'll say it again.
Breakfast is a statement of identity.
Housemade breads, our own preserves,
local cheeses,
farm eggs cooked to order.
Generous, honest, unhurried.
Many guests will tell you a check out
that breakfast was their favorite part of the day.
That's normal.
And it's a compliment to protect.
Lunch and dinner, seasonal, simple, satisfying.
Dishes with character, prepared with care and creativity.
Indoors in the light filled dining room
or outside on the terrace
with the garden and the Alentejo evening.
And the pizzas.
Let's talk about the pizzas
because guests certainly will.
The outdoor wood-fired oven
is one of the most beloved things on this property.
Sun-ripened tomatoes, just-picked herbs,
local cheeses, fire.
Children make their own in the pizza classes
and eat their creation with the pride you can photograph.
Never look down on the pizza because it's humble.
The wood-fired pizza on a summer evening.
Kids running on the grass, fire pits starting to glow.
That image is crevairal, working at full power.
Wine, you know my weakness.
Our list celebrates Alentejo.
The bold reds, the balanced whites, the artisanal blends.
And I want every front-of-house person
to be able to guide a guest through it without fear.
You don't need to be a sommelier.
You need three sentences per wine,
where it's from, what it's like,
what it loves to be eaten with.
This white comes from vineyards near the coast,
20 minutes from here.
It's fresh, a little saline.
And it's exactly what the fish wants.
That's it.
That sentence sells the wine, honors the winemaker,
and deepens the guest's connection to the territory.
Three sentences.
And fermentation, preservation, the old arts.
Our preserves, our jams, the pickles,
the way we extend the garden's abundance across the seasons.
This is ancestral intelligence.
The circular economy existed in every Alentejo pantry
long before anyone gave it a name.
When you explain to a guest that this jam exists
because the orchard gave us more fruit in July
than we could serve fresh,
you're teaching regeneration with a spoon.
Now, service at the farm table.
A few principles I hold hard.
Never rush a table.
We are the antidote to the city,
and the long meal is the ceremony of this place.
The table under the stars, the second bottle,
the conversation that stretches.
Protect it.
Efficiency matters in the kitchen.
At the table, presence matters more.
Tell the chain.
Every dish has a story, and the story is true.
Use it.
Not a lecture, one line.
The courgettes are from the garden, picked this morning.
One line changes the meal.
Honesty about what we are.
We're not a gastronomic temple with tweezers and foam.
We are honest, excellent, soulful cooking from a working farm.
Own that identity with pride.
The guest who wants a Michelin performance has other addresses.
The guest who wants to taste the territory has us.
And there are many, many more of the second kind.
Dietary needs are hospitality, not hassle.
Allergies, intolerances, vegetarians,
children who eat nothing but pasta.
Every one of these is a person hoping not to be a problem.
Make them feel like they're not.
The kitchen that improvises a beautiful vegetarian plate
without sighing has just won a family's loyalty forever.
And remember, the farm table is also the village's table.
In a sense, the restaurant, the events, the catering
that takes our kitchen to weddings and companies.
A maize du camp taking this territory's cuisine
to a museum in Lisbon.
One kitchen philosophy, many tables.
The gesture, always the same.
Bring those who eat closer to those who grow.
Last thought for this model.
Food is where trust becomes physical.
A guest answers their hunger three times a day.
There's something ancient and intimate about that.
Feed people like you, mean it.
Because here, we do.
Next module, the constellation beyond the farm,
the beach bar, Lisbon, events.
And how it all holds together.
